frameworks.name: Four Elements of Equity
frameworks.definition: Equity structure can be decomposed into four independent dimensions—control (decision authority), risk (liability if failure), profits (cash flow distributions), and enterprise value (upside at sale or liquidity event)—each of which can be contracted separately rather than bundled in shares.

frameworks.name: Investment-Focused Talent Pitch
frameworks.definition: Recruiting early hires or co-founders is fundamentally a capital-raising pitch, except the investor is deploying time, expertise, and life energy instead of cash; the sales mechanism is identical to investor pitch.

claims.text: Exceptional talent with high current compensation and job security requires either cash compensation, equity upside, or contractual claims on profit or enterprise value to justify leaving their existing role; compensation is the structural lever available when a startup cannot match salary.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: startup has capital constraints relative to prospect's current role
claims.mechanism: equity or profit claims provide upside participation that salary alone cannot match
bounded_by: Does not apply to talent seeking primarily salary increases or lifestyle improvements without upside participation

claims.text: In non-software businesses, equity can be structured by decomposing control (decision-making authority), risk (liability exposure), profits (cash distributions), and enterprise value (liquidity upside) as separate contractual dimensions rather than bundling all four into stock shares.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: separable equity components allow tailoring incentive alignment to individual risk tolerance and value preference, reducing total cash outlay while maintaining upside motivation
bounded_by: Assumes legal flexibility to contract around standard equity templates; not all jurisdictions or investor structures permit this decomposition

claims.text: Prospective hires typically decline full equity risk (liability for downside if business fails) and lack control authority (decision-making power) in founder-led companies; the negotiable levers are therefore profit participation and enterprise-value upside.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: talent aversion to downside risk and desire to preserve founder authority creates a constrained bargaining space where only profit and upside are credible incentives
bounded_by: Does not apply to co-founder relationships where equity is split equally or when external investors require full ownership consolidation

claims.text: Asking the prospect directly 'What would it take?' is a high-leverage recruiting question that surfaces their true value trade-offs and required terms, rather than the recruiter proposing incrementally inadequate offers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect has existing role and compensation
claims.mechanism: the question 'What would it take?' assumes the prospect will accept (affirmative frame) and invites them to specify their true requirement rather than passive rejection; reveals willingness-to-move and actual constraint (compensation vs. role type vs. mission alignment)
bounded_by: Assumes the prospect is open to recruitment; does not work if the prospect has already declined interest or is actively avoiding recruiter contact

claims.text: Recruiting early hires and co-founders uses the same emotional and narrative structure as investor pitching, except the capital being invested is time, expertise, and life energy rather than cash.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect has significant existing opportunity cost
claims.mechanism: both investors and early-stage hires evaluate opportunity cost and conviction in the founder/mission; narrative framing that creates emotional conviction (mission alignment, founder credibility, long-term upside) is the primary persuasion lever in both contexts
bounded_by: Applies to early-stage and high-growth contexts; does not apply to mid-market hiring where role specificity and immediate compensation are primary drivers

claims.text: The Steve Jobs recruiting example (asking John Scully 'Do you want to continue selling sugar water or come change the world?') succeeds because it reframes the decision from a salary/role comparison to a mission-driven aspiration question, activating the prospect's identity and purpose alignment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect is established in a stable, non-mission-driven role
founder has a credible vision and track record
claims.mechanism: positioning the choice as mission-driven rather than role-driven taps into identity alignment and long-term meaning, which outweighs short-term compensation disadvantage when the prospect perceives founder credibility
bounded_by: Requires that the founder has actual credibility and the mission is genuinely differentiated; the framing fails if the prospect perceives the mission as marketing copy or the founder as unproven

examples.text: Steve Jobs recruited John Scully from Pepsi by reframing the decision from continued high-paying commodity work ('selling sugar water') to a mission-driven transformative role ('change the world'), converting a perceived downside (leaving a successful role) into an identity-aligned opportunity.

practices.text: When recruiting high-level talent, ask 'What would it take?' rather than proposing offers; this surfaces their true requirements and frames the conversation as a mutual fit assessment rather than a one-way pitch.

Structure equity discussions by explicitly decompositioning control, risk, profits, and enterprise value as separate contractual levers; clarify which dimensions the prospect values most (e.g., some want profit participation only, others want upside at exit).

When recruiting a co-founder or early leader, pitch the mission and founder credibility as the primary persuasion lever, mimicking the emotional frame of an investor pitch but emphasizing time/expertise investment rather than capital.
